chapter_theme: At Lakkanai's wedding the king's daughter is blessed, bathed and seated in a pearl hall, and a skilled dresser does her hair, brow, eyes, ears, wrists, breasts, girdle, feet and hands, until her beauty disarms Kama and bewilders onlookers, and the household hides her with fans and a parasol.

cast.role: the king's daughter, Lakkanai, the bride being adorned
the skilled woman who dresses the bride's hair and body
the many who bless the bride at the wedding

2428.reading: Water scented with white durva flowers washes the lord's red feet, the faultless auspicious light that was lifted is shown, and the wedding fills with finely worked decoration.
2428.nuance: இறைவன் may be the king giving the bride or the Jina; the verse does not say, so who is honoured is left open.
2428.event: The rite of washing the lord's feet and showing the auspicious light opens the wedding.

2429.reading: Many bless the girl, whose lily eyes are like bright swords drawn from the sheath and who is like the goddess of wealth, and set her on a silver stool and then on a jewelled couch.
2429.event: Many bless the bride and seat her on a silver stool, then a jewelled couch.

2430.reading: They hail her as gold grown on the mountain, a single right-whorled conch-gem, nectar of the waves and the object of Lakshmi's wish, and the fine women put durva grass in ghee on her to the sound of bangles, drums and conches.
2430.event: Women praise the bride and anoint her with ghee and durva grass.

2431.reading: They bathe the king's daughter with clear bathing water brought in a fine jewelled pot on a white musth elephant, and she looks like Lakshmi on a flower.
2431.nuance: The syntax of ஏற்றி (raised, carried) leaves open whether the pot rides the elephant or the girl is lifted to it; the sense of an elephant-borne bath pot matches Gandharvadattai's bath in 623.
2431.event: The bride is given the ceremonial bath with water from a jewelled pot carried on an elephant.

2432.reading: The bath water flows on with flower foam, with gems it does not spill, with scented powder and saffron mixed into mud on the young sand banks, and with bees singing over it.

2433.reading: They seat her in a hall of pearl pillars set with coral under a golden canopy hung with pearl strings, where rays shine like the moon's.
2433.event: The bride is seated under a golden canopy in a pearl hall.

2434.reading: Women with garland-wreathed hair stand about the bride bearing ornaments, garlands and bright cloth, as she sits shaded like a creeper.
2434.event: The attendants gather round the bride with ornaments, garlands and cloth.

2435.reading: The women begin to adorn the soft-voiced girl with bangles, an anklet, the eye-ornament called விலாசி and garlands for the wrist and body.
2435.nuance: விலாசி is a rare word whose sense (an ornament for the eye or brow) is a guess.
2435.event: The attendants begin to dress the bride in ornaments.

2436.reading: Her dresser draws from its sheath, as the moon from cloud, the auspicious comb made from the right tusk of the lord of elephants, set with gold and gems.
2436.event: The dresser takes the ivory comb out of its case.

2437.reading: A woman who knows every treatise parts, gathers and spreads her dark hair according to the hand-books, steeps it in musk paste and agil smoke, and ties it in a knot as handsome as a bull's hump.
2437.nuance: The dresser is named only by her skill in the manuals (கைந்நூல், நூல்); dressing the hair is told as a learned art, as Civakan's dressing of the dancer is in 673.
2437.event: The dresser combs, perfumes and knots the bride's hair by the rules of the craft.

2438.reading: The sweet-worded dresser fastens jasmine and white-flower garlands, sets a gold band like the moon among lightning on the bride's brow, and ties on a golden makara hung with pearls.
2438.event: The dresser sets the flower garlands, forehead band and makara ornament on the bride.

2439.reading: She crushes honey-dripping kuvalai flowers, nips them with her curved nail to print the forehead mark, spreads bright powder on the brow and draws the bride's long heart-drinking eyes in collyrium.
2439.nuance: The finger-and-nail setting of the mark is what Vijayai undoes in 350.
2439.event: The dresser prints the tilaka and paints the eyes with collyrium.

2440.reading: She takes off the bride's ear-studs of tusk and the plain ear-rings and sets in their place gem ear-ornaments that burn like a cloud pouring lightning, so bright that the gods in the sky desire her.
2440.event: The dresser changes the bride's plain ear-ornaments for the gem wedding ear-rings.

2441.reading: Bangles of conch ring on her forearms, coral and gold finger-rings flash, and a pearl from a right-whorled conch on her neck and full shoulders shines like moonlight.
2441.event: The dresser puts bangles, rings and the pearl necklace on the bride.

2442.reading: On breasts like emerald caskets roofed with gems she draws in sandal paste the creeper of desire, flowering and trembling, down her soft shoulders.
2442.nuance: The pattern is called காம வல்லி, the creeper of desire; the poet names the art by the god it serves.
2442.event: The dresser paints the sandal-paste creeper on the bride's breasts and shoulders.

2443.reading: Seeing her waist ache under its smiling lightning and the gold chain roll free of its weight, Kama forgets his bee-song bow and arrows, says he cannot bear to look, melts and hides his body.
2443.nuance: நாண்சுமக்கலாத is hard (she who bears no shame or no bow-string); the sense that her beauty disarms the love-god is clear either way.
2443.event: Kama, seeing the adorned bride, forgets his arrows and hides himself.

2444.reading: She puts on a girdle of gems whose rays loosen the life of those who look, and a silk their eyes cannot hold, so that she looks like the full moon wearing its own soft rays.
2444.event: The dresser girdles the bride and clothes her in fine silk.

2445.reading: Thigh-bands, tinkling anklets and gem toe-rings go on, and she is made to sit among garlands.
2445.nuance: Lines 3-4 (நாகத் துடைச் சிறு நாவில் தோகை) are hard to construe and the last clause is a guess.
2445.event: The dresser puts thigh, ankle and toe ornaments on the bride and seats her among garlands.

2446.reading: The dresser paints the soft feet, hands and mouth of the girl with red lac and finishes the bride.
2446.nuance: வலத்தகம் is probably a misprint for அலத்தகம், the red lac.
2446.event: The dresser paints the bride's hands and feet with lac.

2447.reading: The bangled women look at her bright eyes, her breasts, her hips and the knot of her hair in turn and stand with a man's longing for her.
2447.nuance: The women, not men, are said to feel ஆண்விருப்பு; the poem lets the dressing itself show how great the beauty is.
2447.event: The attendants stand gazing at the bride with longing.

2448.reading: The narrator says that even her maker, if he saw her, would be bewildered, and even the unbewildered would reel, so how could those in the sickness of delusion escape; such was how the graceless ones adorned her beauty.
2448.nuance: இருளிலார் and அருளிலார் in lines 3-4 can be read in more than one way (those free of darkness, those without compassion); the narrator's point is the overpowering of the heart by beauty.

claims.claim: a woman's adorned beauty can bewilder even those not given to bewilderment

2449.reading: Fully adorned she stands like a gem branch of the wishing tree blossoming in gold, her body shining with lightning, as though the lotus-goddess had left the opened lotus in a sulk, her eyes red.

2450.reading: Her flowered hair looks as if a skilled maker of jasmine garlands had strung it with cuts of darkness between the flowers and gathered scrolls of white moonlight in one place.

2451.reading: Death has come in the form of the king's daughter, and her girdle, anklet and bells cry with their own mouths to the onlookers to go while they can, keeping their lives and guarding their hearts.
2451.nuance: The warning is spoken by her ornaments, the same cry that onlookers put in the ornaments' mouths for Gandharvadattai in 637.

2452.reading: Fearing that even the graceless, though like Hara, would reel and make the world roll today, the chowries, sandal fans and white parasol hide the girl.
2452.nuance: The sense of அருளிலார் இவடம் அரன்னராயினும் is uncertain; the plain act, fans and parasol screening her, is clear.
2452.event: The attendants shade the bride with fans and a parasol to hide her.

links.note: The onlookers of 637 say the bride's girdle and breasts are Death upon Death and that the anklet bells cry to the suitors to run and save their lives; here Death has come in the king's daughter's form and her girdle, anklet and bells cry to the onlookers to go and guard their hearts.
links.teaches: The cry that was gossip at Gandharvadattai's contest becomes the ornaments' own speech at Lakkanai's wedding, so the adornment itself is made the warning.

links.note: Kural 1083 has a man say he never knew Death and now does, it being a woman's grace and large war-eyes; 2451 says Death has come in a king's daughter's form and her own jewels bid the onlookers flee.
links.teaches: The couplet turns Death into one man's private discovery, while the epic makes it a public warning given by the jewels, so a figure of suffering becomes a danger announced to a crowd.

gains.a: a source for the figure of the woman as Death, which shows the jewels' warning is a figure for the pain beauty gives and not an idle boast
gains.b: a scene of bride, ornaments and a watching crowd that shows what in her dress the poet reads as a weapon, which the couplet leaves to the word பெண்டகை

links.note: The dresser nips flowers with her curved nail to print the bride's forehead mark, the opening of a householder's life; Vijayai, turning ascetic, takes the mark off with her finger, with the ear-rings and pearls, to close it.
links.teaches: The same mark and the same ornaments are put on to begin a marriage and taken off to end a life in the world, so the epic shows adornment as the sign of entry and renunciation as its undoing.

links.note: The dresser takes off the bride's tusk studs and plain ear-rings and sets wedding ear-ornaments (கடிப்பு); the herdswomen take off the herd girl's gold ear-studs and gem pendants and set the same auspicious கடிப்பு with a small simple adornment.
links.teaches: The same step in the rite is done in the same words for a king's daughter and a herd girl, showing the rite fixed while the stuff of the ornaments shows the wealth of the house.

links.note: Civakan adorns the dancer by the stage rules, tying the band, crowning, setting sandal and jewels; the bride's dresser, who knows every treatise, dresses the bride's hair by the hand-books.
links.teaches: Both scenes make dressing a learned craft with its manuals, so Lakkanai's toilet is told as an art practised by a master and not as vanity.

links.note: Gandharvadattai is bathed in scented water brought in gem pots on elephants' heads; the king's daughter is bathed with water in a jewelled pot on a white musth elephant.
links.teaches: The bath on an elephant's pot is the royal bride's rite in two marriages, which marks Lakkanai's wedding as one in the line of the contest bride's.

links.note: The city women take Civakan for Kama who has put down his arrows and come in person; here Kama himself forgets his bow and arrows before the adorned bride and hides.
links.teaches: The poem gives the hero the god's looks, then lets the bride overcome the god, which sets her beauty above the hero's.

links.note: The dresser draws the creeper of desire in sandal paste on the bride's breasts; the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the body when the axle of its cart breaks.
links.teaches: The painted creeper is told as a high art at its best, so the Naladiyar's corpse image is shown to answer not coarse adornment but the finest.

gains.a: the other side of the sandal-paste art, the body that lies under it, which the tender scene never looks at
gains.b: a worked scene of sandal and garland laid on with great skill, which shows what its warning is aimed at and why it needs saying

links.note: The narrator says her adorned beauty would bewilder even the steady; the Tirumanthiram tells the heart to turn from women who smile and show their breasts, as the etti tree's fruit is good to look at and not to eat.
links.teaches: The narrator and the Saiva teacher agree that adorned beauty overcomes the heart, but the narrator offers it as wonder and the teacher as a poison to resist.

gains.a: a remedy, the turning away of the heart, which the narrator names as a sickness but does not prescribe for
gains.b: an instance of beauty so dressed and so praised that the warning is tested against the strongest case, not left as a general rule

links.note: The bangled women stand desiring the bride's eyes, breasts, hips and hair; the Naladiyar tells the reader not to desire a woman for her spear-like eyes, for she too will stoop and walk with a staff for eyes.
links.teaches: The gaze that the epic lingers on is the one the Naladiyar answers with the staff of old age, giving the scene's longing a time it will pass through.

gains.a: a limit of time on the beauty so intently looked at, which the scene itself does not offer
gains.b: a particular pair of eyes, hips and hair worth the longing the quatrain says to resist, so its warning has something to weigh against

links.note: After the ornaments cry that Death has come, the chowries, sandal fans and white parasol hide the girl for fear of what the graceless would do to the rolling world.
links.teaches: The screening is the household's answer to the danger the ornaments announce, so the verse before it is read as a threat to be guarded against and not praise only.

source_issues: 2437-2447 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2446 line 3 வலத்தகம் is probably a misprint for அலத்தகம்.
2443 line 1 நாண்சுமக்கலாத, 2445 lines 3-4 and 2435 விலாசி are hard to construe.
2448 lines 3-4 இருளிலார் and அருளிலார் can be read more than one way.
